issue: Source: "more or at least as much might have been hazarded by taking the system of any one State for a standard, as by omitting a provision altogether". Candidate: "Second, as much, or at least as much, might have been risked..." drops "more" (the comparative claim is weakened and the phrase reads as a duplication).
replacement: From this sketch it appears that there is a material diversity, in the form as well as in the extent of the institution of trial by jury in civil cases, among the individual States. Two obvious reflections follow from this fact. First, the Convention could not have fixed upon any general rule that would have suited the circumstances of all the States. Second, more, or at least as much, might have been risked by taking the system of any one State as a standard than by omitting a provision altogether and leaving the matter, as has been done, to legislative regulation.

issue: Source: "They have tended to show that ...; that even in far the greatest proportion ...; that it is in no case abolished(3) ...; and that there are great ... difficulties". Candidate turns the hedged "tended to show" into "They have shown" for the 2nd and 3rd points (modal strength raised; Hamilton's qualifier lost).
replacement: On the other hand, I cannot help believing that the different lights in which the subject has been placed in these observations will go far toward removing the apprehensions that open-minded persons may have felt about it. They have tended to show that the security of liberty is materially at stake only in trial by jury in criminal cases, which the plan of the Convention provides for in the most ample manner. They have also tended to show that, in by far the greatest proportion of civil cases, and in those that concern the great body of the community, that mode of trial will stay in full force as established by the State constitutions, untouched and unaffected by the plan of the Convention. They have further tended to show that the plan abolishes it(3) in no case, and that there are great, if not insurmountable, difficulties in the way of making any precise and proper provision for it in a Constitution for the United States.

issue: Source: "the general GENIUS of a government". Candidate leaves archaic "GENIUS" (STYLE-NOTE table: genius of a government -> character/spirit). A general reader will read it as talent. Keep the emphasis capitals on the replacement word.
replacement: This is now clearly understood to be the case in Great Britain, and it is equally so in the State of Connecticut. Yet it can safely be affirmed that more encroachments on trial by jury have been made in this State since the Revolution, although a positive article of our constitution provides for it, than in the same time in either Connecticut or Great Britain. It may be added that these encroachments have generally begun with the men who try to persuade the people that they are the warmest defenders of popular liberty, but who have seldom allowed constitutional obstacles to stop them in a favorite course. The truth is that the general CHARACTER of a government is all that can be substantially relied upon for lasting effects. Particular provisions, though not altogether useless, have far less virtue and effectiveness than are commonly ascribed to them; and the want of them will never be, with men of sound discernment, a decisive objection to any plan that shows the leading characters of a good government.

issue: Source: "It certainly sounds not a little harsh and extraordinary". Candidate: "certainly sounds harsh and extraordinary" drops the intensifier "not a little" (force softened).
replacement: It certainly sounds more than a little harsh and extraordinary to claim that a Constitution offers no security for liberty, though it expressly establishes trial by jury in criminal cases, merely because it does not do so in civil cases too. Meanwhile it is notorious that Connecticut, always regarded as the most popular State in the Union, can boast of no constitutional provision for either.

issue: Source: "The latter has made requisitions which the former have had to provide for." Candidate leaves "requisitions" unglossed; STYLE-NOTE asks for a short gloss the first time it appears in a paper where the sentence needs it, and a general reader will not know the term.
replacement: But there is another circumstance of great importance from the standpoint of economy. The business of the United States has so far occupied the State legislatures as well as Congress. Congress has made requisitions, or formal requests for money, which the State legislatures have had to provide for. As a result, the sessions of the State legislatures have been prolonged far beyond what was necessary to carry out the merely local business of the States. More than half their time has frequently been spent on matters relating to the United States. Now the members who make up the legislatures of the individual States number two thousand and upward, and this body has so far performed what under the new system will be done at first by sixty-five persons, and probably at no later period by more than a fourth or fifth of that number. Under the proposed government, Congress will itself do all the business of the United States, without the intervention of the State legislatures. From then on the latter will have only the affairs of their own States to attend to, and will not have to sit for anything like as long as they have until now. This difference in the length of the State legislatures' sessions will be clear gain, and by itself will make up a saving that may be regarded as an equivalent for any additional expenses the new system may occasion.

issue: Footnote 3, corrupt source: "it is evident that the extent must depend on legislative discretion, respecting the liberty of the press, will give it no greater security than it will have without them." Candidate invents "and declarations" (and "their extent") to repair it, silently smoothing a source defect. Render the clause as the source stands and list it as an open issue. Also restores source order "the press nowhere enjoys greater liberty".
replacement: 3. To show that the Constitution contains a power by which the liberty of the press may be affected, people have turned to the power of taxation. It is said that duties may be laid on publications so high as to amount to a prohibition. I do not know by what logic it could be maintained that the declarations in the State constitutions in favor of freedom of the press would be a constitutional obstacle to the State legislatures' imposing duties on publications. It certainly cannot be pretended that any degree of duties, however low, would be an abridgment of the liberty of the press. We know that newspapers are taxed in Great Britain, and yet it is notorious that the press nowhere enjoys greater liberty than in that country. And if duties of any kind may be laid without violating that liberty, it is evident that the extent must depend on legislative discretion, respecting the liberty of the press, will give it no greater security than it will have without them. The same invasions of it may be carried out through taxation under the State constitutions that contain those declarations as under the proposed Constitution, which has nothing of the kind. It would be quite as meaningful to declare that government ought to be free, that taxes ought not to be excessive, etc., as that the liberty of the press ought not to be restrained.

issue: Source: "whether ... the proposed Constitution has not been satisfactorily vindicated ...; and whether it has not been shown to be worthy". Candidate turns Publius's leading negative questions into neutral ones ("has ... been satisfactorily defended"), losing the rhetorical push.
replacement: Let us now pause and ask ourselves whether, over the course of these papers, the proposed Constitution has not been satisfactorily defended against the slurs cast on it, and whether it has not been shown to deserve public approval and to be necessary for the public safety and prosperity. Every man is bound to answer these questions to himself as honestly as his conscience and understanding allow, and then to act on the real and sober verdict of his judgment. Nothing can release him from this duty. All the obligations that hold society together call on him, indeed compel him, to carry it out sincerely and honestly. No biased motive, no private interest, no pride in his own opinion, no passing passion or prejudice can justify to himself, to his country or to his descendants a wrong choice of the part he is to play. Let him beware of stubbornly sticking to a party. Let him reflect that what he must decide is not some particular interest of the community but the very existence of the nation. And let him remember that a majority of America has already given its approval to the plan he is now to accept or reject.

issue: Source: "far more easy to obtain subsequent than previous amendments" (i.e. after adoption than before). Candidate "later amendments ... than earlier ones" reads as later-versus-earlier amendments, not after-versus-before adoption; the key point of the argument is ambiguous.
replacement: It appears to me capable of absolute demonstration that it will be far easier to obtain amendments to the Constitution after it is adopted than before. The moment an alteration is made in the present plan, it becomes, for the purpose of adoption, a new plan, and must undergo a new decision by each State. Its complete establishment throughout the Union will therefore require the concurrence of thirteen States. If, on the contrary, the proposed Constitution is once ratified by all the States as it stands, alterations in it may be made at any time by nine States. Here, then, the chances are as thirteen to nine(2) in favor of later amendment rather than of the original adoption of an entire system.
